verdict.root_cause: cartservice requests are blocked on Redis: HGET and HMSET client spans each cost ~300-306ms with almost no variance while cartservice handler self-time is under ~1.5ms [tr_28516a3e7b4d]. Reads and writes are equally affected and cost scales with operation count, not load, which is the signature of a fixed delay inserted into the cartservice-to-redis-cart network path. The change record documents exactly that mechanism as recurring automation on this service: a traffic-shaping container attached to the cart-service network namespace with a fixed egress delay [tr_b19a0cf4a3a4]. cartservice itself is healthy, serving cart operations continuously with no errors or lifecycle events [tr_ac10a806d663], and no span carries an error status [tr_28516a3e7b4d]. The latency propagates upward into frontend GET (~305-310ms) and POST (~906-921ms) flows, which explains why frontend, checkoutservice and loadgenerator alerted 15 seconds later without error-rate rises of their own [tr_330cf881f56b].
verdict.reasoning: Traces localise all elapsed time inside the cartservice Redis client spans, excluding the frontend, the gRPC hop, sibling microservices (sub-ms to ~11ms) and cartservice's own CPU work [tr_28516a3e7b4d]. Among cache-path explanations, the tight ~5ms band around 300ms with writes equal to reads indicates a constant additive delay rather than server-side queueing or contention [tr_28516a3e7b4d], and the change history independently records a fixed egress delay shaper on the cart-service namespace [tr_b19a0cf4a3a4]. I chose dependency_latency over bad_config because the failing mechanism is the wait - requests succeed, just slowly - and a setting that inserts delay into a call path is a latency fault. Not resource_exhaustion: nothing ran out and serving is uninterrupted [tr_ac10a806d663]. Not bad_deploy: image applies were reverted and cartservice ran its baseline image at onset [tr_b19a0cf4a3a4]. Confidence is medium because the change log claims the shaper was removed ~2h before onset with nothing landing in the hour prior, yet the delay is measurably present at 23:24; the direct measurement outweighs an untrusted, possibly incomplete record.
open_questions: Whether the traffic shaper was re-attached after its recorded removal - the change log's claim of no change in the hour before onset contradicts the observed delay at 23:24.
redis-cart was never dispatched against, so no server-side latency, memory or connection evidence exists to exclude a ~300ms Redis-side floor.

Trace coverage is a single ~14-second slice at 23:24:21-23:24:34, so onset time and whether the delay has cleared are unestablished; cartservice also has no call metrics in either window [tr_34b8a8ef0ecb], leaving no latency baseline.

alternatives.root_cause: redis-cart itself became uniformly slow, adding ~300ms to every operation from the server side.
alternatives.why_not: A loaded or degraded server produces skewed, variable latency; the observed spread is ~5ms around 300ms for both reads and writes [tr_28516a3e7b4d], and no change or fault was recorded against redis-cart while a fixed-delay shaper was recorded against cartservice [tr_b19a0cf4a3a4].

alternatives.root_cause: A REDIS_ADDR override left cartservice talking to a distant or wrong redis-cart endpoint, adding round-trip cost.
alternatives.why_not: Every REDIS_ADDR override was reverted, the last 1.7h before onset [tr_b19a0cf4a3a4], and cart operations succeed with no connection errors [tr_ac10a806d663]; a wrong endpoint would more likely fail than uniformly delay.

proposal.expected_effect: No action proposed, so no effect is predicted. What should happen next is observation, not change: re-query Tempo for cartservice traces outside the single 23:24:21-23:24:34 slice, and dispatch against redis-cart for server-side latency, to establish whether the ~300ms per-operation floor is still present and whether it is inside redis-cart or in the network path to it. Either answer is directly observable - HGET/HMSET client span duration in Tempo, and Redis-side command latency - and either one would unlock a defensible action.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention is wrong if evidence appears that a cartservice configuration or environment value was applied and left in effect inside the incident window - for example a change-history entry showing a REDIS_ADDR override or traffic-shaper attach after 22:25 with no matching revert, or a redis-cart dispatch showing sub-millisecond server-side command latency while client spans stay at ~300ms and a namespace attachment is confirmed live. Any of those would meet revert_config's second precondition and make a config_revert on cartservice the right call. It is also wrong if the delay is still active and each minute of it is costing checkout conversion badly enough that acting on a medium-confidence read beats waiting for two cheap queries - that is a judgement for the reader, not for me.
proposal.risk: The risk of abstaining is that a live ~300ms-per-Redis-operation delay continues, keeping frontend GET at ~305-310ms and POST at ~906-921ms [tr_28516a3e7b4d] for as long as it takes to gather the missing evidence. That is real user-visible harm and it is not zero. I am accepting it because every permitted action here fails its own preconditions: revert_config requires the evidence to name a configuration change inside the incident window, and the change record states the opposite - the traffic-shaping container was removed 2.0h before onset, the last REDIS_ADDR revert landed 1.7h before onset, and every apply in the window has a matching revert [tr_b19a0cf4a3a4]. Reverting cartservice to a 'prior configuration' that the record says is already the running configuration would recreate the container for no modelled reason, and if the shaper is in fact re-attached out-of-band, a config revert does not detach a sidecar bound to the network namespace - it would recreate cartservice, look like it worked or did not, and leave the actual mechanism unexplained. rollback_image is ruled out: no deploy or image change is named inside the window, and both image applies were reverted 2.3h prior [tr_b19a0cf4a3a4]. restart_service requires the evidence to point at process state, and it points the other way - cartservice handler self-time is under ~1.5ms, no error spans, continuous clean request logging with no lifecycle events [tr_28516a3e7b4d, tr_ac10a806d663]. scale_service is unavailable in this world.
proposal.blast_radius: None from this proposal, since nothing changes. For context on what a rejected action would have touched: any recreate of cartservice resets connections for frontend and checkoutservice, which are its named inbound callers, and loadgenerator sees it through frontend - all four already alerted. A further complication for anyone who acts anyway: cartservice has no calls_total samples in either window [tr_34b8a8ef0ecb], so there is no Prometheus latency or error baseline to confirm recovery against; verification would have to come from Tempo span durations and Loki request continuity, and the absence of a metric baseline is itself a reason to prefer measurement over action right now.

triage_judgement.reasoning: Multiple services alerting within seconds along the cart/checkout/frontend path, not a single isolated warning, so it cannot be dismissed. The fan-out pattern starting at cartservice and spreading upstream suggests a shared dependency slowdown, though the class is only a prior.
